For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: μ = tan θₚ is self-consistent with Snell's law — sin θₚ = μ sin r together with θₚ + r = 90° gives sin θₚ = μ cos θₚ, hence μ = tan θₚ; at the polarising angle the reflected light is completely plane polarised and the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.
insider_note: Most students write μ = tan θₚ and stop — the perpendicular reflected and refracted rays are the other half of the answer.

steps.margin_note: First mark. Define the polarising angle before using it — it is the angle at which the reflected light is completely polarised.
steps.why: Brewster's law is a statement about one special angle, so the answer must first say what is special about it: only at θₚ is the reflected light completely plane polarised. At every other angle it is only partly polarised.
common_mistakes: Saying the reflected light is polarised at every angle. Complete polarisation happens only at the polarising angle.
Saying the refracted light is completely polarised. It is the reflected light; the refracted light stays partly polarised.

recall.must_convey: That at one particular angle of incidence, the polarising angle, the reflected light is completely plane polarised.
accept: at the polarising angle the reflected light is fully polarised

steps.memory_tip: One special angle, one special result: at θₚ the REFLECTED light is completely polarised.

steps.margin_note: Second mark. Write the formula AND the perpendicularity — they belong together, one follows from the other.
steps.why: The tangent form is not an extra fact to memorise: put r = 90° − θₚ into Snell's law sin θₚ = μ sin r and μ = tan θₚ drops out. Writing the perpendicular rays next to the formula shows the examiner the law is understood, not copied.
common_mistakes: Writing μ = tan θ with an unnamed angle. The angle in the law is the polarising angle θₚ.
Leaving out the perpendicular reflected and refracted rays, which is the condition the formula comes from.

recall.must_convey: That μ equals tan of the polarising angle, and at that angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.
